data.title: Exclusive: Daytona, a startup building the ‘agentic cloud,’ valued at $1 billion in funding round
data.ai_summary: Daytona raised $60 million in a Series B round at a $1 billion valuation, led by FirstMark. The San Francisco startup provides sandboxes for AI agents, provisioning them in 60 milliseconds. It plans to use the funds for hiring sales staff and engineers.
data.author: Jeremy Kahn

industries.name: LLMOps & Generative AI Platforms (Prompt/Agent Orchestration, RAG)
Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text:
AI agents need somewhere to work—and Ivan Burazin thinks the existing cloud providers aren’t the right answer. Now Burazin, the cofounder and CEO of Daytona, a San Francisco-based startup, has turned the idea of a new kind of cloud just for AI agents into a unicorn business.

Recommended Video

Daytona said Tuesday it has raised a $60 million Series B venture capital round at a $1 billion valuation. FirstMark led the round. It was joined by an A-list roster of Silicon Valley founders, including Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo and Zoom’s Eric Yuan, plus strategic investors Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next and Okta Ventures. Burazin told Fortune that about $50 million of the round came from existing investors. The new funding brings the amount Daytona has raised to date to about $91 million. Why agents need their own computers An AI agent that writes and runs code, browses the web or operates business software needs to use a computer—either an actual machine, or a virtual one, running in the cloud. For many use cases, having a virtual machine is preferable—it allows the AI agent to operate even if the person running the agent shuts down their laptop, and because virtual machines can be configured with only the software and network access the agent needs to do a particular task and nothing more, it is generally a safer way to run AI agents. A virtual machine, or “sandbox” as they are sometimes called, minimizes the chance that the agent will run amok and take damaging unauthorized actions, or that an outside party could hijack the agent and get it to divulge sensitive data. Daytona was founded in 2023 by Burazin, Goran Draganić and Vedran Jukić to automate software development environments for large enterprises. When the founders saw that agents would need computers too, Burazin said, they “basically gave our competitors all our customers, rebuilt everything, had like three months left of revenue in the bank, and then relaunched this thing.” Daytona currently provides these sandboxes to many of the leading AI companies, which use the virtual machines to allow their models to practice tasks over and over inside sandboxes during training and testing. Daytona says AI data company Snorkel, which also helps customers test and benchmark AI models, has provisioned more than one million sandboxes on its platform. It also counts Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia, Cursor, Cognition, Meta and Cohere among its customers.



Burazin said that Daytona’s revenue run rate grew 25-fold between January and September. “We’ve been growing on average every single month 50.9%,” Burazin said. Existing cloud providers, such as Amazon’s AWS, Microsoft’s Azure, or Google’s Google Cloud Platform, allow customers to spin up virtual machines. But doing so takes between 30 seconds and many minutes, depending on the complexity of the configuration. This, Burazin said, is far too long for the future of agentic work, when companies may be deploying thousands or even tens of thousands of AI agents, each of which may need access to different software tools depending on the task they are being asked to complete.



Daytona can configure a new sandbox for an AI agent in 60 milliseconds, according to Burazin. That is roughly half the time it takes to blink. The trick, he said, is to pre-distribute snapshots of configured machines onto the physical drives of servers. When an agent needs a machine, Daytona attaches processing power and memory and resumes the snapshot. Agents can also clone a running computer to try different approaches in parallel. “You can literally replicate the computer into two and try both outcomes, and then replicate again and again and again until it gets the desired outcome,” Burazin said. When he pitched investors, Burazin said, many asked “why the hell do we need this? You know, AWS can do this thing.” His answer is that hyperscalers built nearly everything on a few core services optimized for maximum utilization. To match Daytona’s performance, he argued, they would need to create a whole new company inside their existing cloud services. He conceded the hyperscalers could do this, but said it would not be easy for them to rebuild their infrastructure to serve AI agents instead of human users. The scale involved is easy to underestimate. Burazin pointed to Muse, the personal agent Meta launched in September. He said it has “a computer underneath for every single chat.” By his back-of-the-envelope math, Muse would need $2.8 billion worth of sandboxes to serve 100 million users. “We believe the next infrastructure shift is from human-centric cloud primitives to agent-native ones,” Matt Turck, a partner at FirstMark, said in a statement. AI models run on GPUs. But to do work, they need CPUs. Burazin also distinguishes what Daytona is building from the “neocloud” providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius. Those neoclouds are designed to train and run AI models. The data centers they are standing up are stuff full of graphics processing units, or GPUs, the computer chips optimized to run AI models. But to run virtual machines, a data center needs lots of traditional central processing units, or CPUs, that can run all kinds of different software. “The inference clouds is where the agent thinks, and our cloud is where the agent works,” Burazin said. “We internally sort of believe that the number of dollars spent on CPUs will probably be higher than the dollars spent on GPUs in the foreseeable future,” he said, “which seems sort of counterintuitive today.”



The demand is so great that he forecasts a coming CPU shortage. “I strongly believe that there will be a CPU crunch,” he said. “The amount of CPU machines that we will need if we want to keep growing at this trajectory actually doesn’t exist right now.” Chipmakers are seeing the same trend. On AMD’s first-quarter earnings call in May, CEO Lisa Su said agentic AI was increasing the need for server CPUs. AMD raised its forecast for server CPU market growth from about 18% a year to more than 35%, reaching over $120 billion by 2030. Chip designer Arm has estimated that agentic AI data centers could need 120 million CPU cores per gigawatt, four times what traditional data centers require. Intel told some Chinese customers earlier this year that lead times for certain server CPUs had stretched to six months, Quartz reported. Burazin said Daytona plans to spend most of the new funds it has raised on hiring go-to-market sales staff, plus some engineers.

data.title: Snorkel AI Raises $350 Million. The Company Building the Data Factory Behind Every Frontier AI Model Just Tripled Its Valuation. - BestStartup.co.uk
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million in a Series E at a $3.5 billion valuation on September 22, 2026, co-led by Insight Partners and S32. Its annualised revenue run rate reached $375 million, an eighteenfold increase in twelve months. The company builds training datasets and evaluation frameworks for frontier AI labs and enterprises.
data.author: Laura Anderson
data.full_text:
Every AI product being built by a UK startup or enterprise right now depends on training data. The large language models they fine-tune, the foundation models they build on, the evaluation benchmarks they use to measure quality all of it was built on data that someone had to construct, curate and validate. Most of the time, that someone is Snorkel AI. Follow every UK startup and tech story at BestStartup UK.
On September 22 2026, Snorkel AI raised $350 million in a Series E at a $3.5 billion valuation, co-led by Insight Partners and S32. Its annualised revenue run rate reached $375 million an eighteenfold increase in twelve months. For context: twelve months ago Snorkel AI was generating approximately $20 million in annualised revenue. Today it is generating $375 million. That is the pace at which frontier AI data demand is growing.
What This Means for UK AI Companies
UK artificial intelligence is a £16 billion sector and growing. DeepMind, Wayve, Stability AI, Synthesia, Darktrace and dozens of other UK AI companies are building products that require training data, evaluation frameworks and reinforcement learning environments to function. Many of them particularly the ones building on or fine-tuning foundation models are already customers or potential customers of the infrastructure Snorkel AI provides.
The broader implication for UK AI founders is that the training data layer is not a commodity. It is a specialised capability that requires deep technical expertise, domain knowledge and the ability to construct expert-level datasets at scale. Snorkel AI’s 18x revenue growth tells you that frontier AI labs and large enterprises have concluded they cannot build this capability internally at the speed and quality they require and are willing to pay premium prices to a specialist supplier who can. Read more UK tech and AI startup stories at BestStartup UK.
What Snorkel AI Actually Builds
Snorkel AI describes itself as the frontier AI data lab. It builds training datasets, evaluation frameworks, synthetic data environments and reinforcement learning setups for AI systems that need more than publicly available data to reach frontier capability.
The shift from its original positioning as a data labelling automation tool to its current positioning as a finished data products company is significant. Labelling automation helped companies create their own data faster. Finished data products means Snorkel creates expert-constructed datasets covering specific domains, capabilities and evaluation benchmarks that frontier AI labs and large enterprises cannot easily produce internally and that take even the most qualified humans hours or days to construct individually. Snorkel AI has built the factory that produces these at scale, reliably, and with the quality controls that frontier model training requires. The Investor Base Behind the Round
New investors in Snorkel AI’s Series E include March Capital, Blumberg Capital, Allegis Capital, Frontline, Standard and Third Point Ventures. Existing investors Greylock, Lightspeed, GV, Addition, Wells Fargo and Walden Catalyst all participated. The participation of Frontline a European venture fund signals that the European and UK investment community is paying close attention to AI infrastructure companies at growth stage, even when those companies are headquartered in San Francisco.

data.title: Snorkel AI Raises $350 Million at $3.5 Billion. Revenue Grew 18x in 12 Months. This Is What AI Infrastructure Actually Looks Like. - Best Startup US
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million in a Series E funding round at a $3.5 billion valuation on September 22, 2026, co-led by Insight Partners and S32. The company reported an annualized revenue run rate of $375 million, marking an eighteenfold increase over the previous twelve months. As a supplier of specialized training datasets and evaluation frameworks for frontier AI labs, Snorkel is expanding capacity to meet growing demand for high-quality AI infrastructure.
data.author: Best Startup
data.full_text:
Every frontier AI model that exists today was trained on data. Every improvement to those models — every new capability, every reduction in hallucination, every increase in reasoning accuracy — required more data, better data, and more precisely constructed training environments. The companies building those frontier models do not build their own training data. They buy it, commission it, and increasingly depend on a small number of specialised suppliers who can deliver the quality and scale they require.
Snorkel AI is the dominant player in that supply chain. On September 22 2026, the San Francisco company raised $350 million in a Series E at a $3.5 billion valuation, co-led by Insight Partners and S32. Follow every US startup funding story at BestStartup US.
The Revenue Number That Explains Everything
Snorkel AI’s annualized revenue run rate reached $375 million in September 2026. Twelve months earlier, that number was approximately $20 million. That is an eighteenfold increase in twelve months — a growth rate that almost never occurs in enterprise software, and almost certainly never occurs in a company that builds physical infrastructure for AI training rather than a pure software product.
The valuation of $3.5 billion represents a 9.3 times revenue multiple — modest by frontier AI standards, aggressive by traditional enterprise software benchmarks. The investor base reflects that positioning. New investors in this round include March Capital, Blumberg Capital, Allegis Capital, Frontline, Standard and Third Point Ventures. Existing investors Greylock, Lightspeed, GV, Addition, Wells Fargo and Walden Catalyst also participated. Read more US AI startup funding stories at BestStartup US.
What Snorkel AI Actually Builds
Snorkel AI describes itself as the frontier AI data lab. That label is precise. The company builds training datasets, evaluation frameworks, synthetic data environments and reinforcement learning setups for AI systems that require more than generic publicly available data to reach frontier capability.
The shift from its original positioning as a labelling automation tool to its current positioning as a finished data products company is significant. Labelling automation helped companies create their own training data faster. Finished data products means Snorkel creates the data itself — expert-constructed datasets covering specific domains, capabilities and evaluation benchmarks that frontier AI labs cannot easily produce internally at the speed and quality they require.
Today’s frontier and agentic AI systems demand what Snorkel calls Data 2.0 — expert agentic tasks, environments and evaluation rubrics that take even the most qualified humans hours or days to construct individually. Snorkel has built the factory that produces these at scale. Its customers include frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, US government agencies and large enterprises. Follow every AI infrastructure story at BestStartup US.
Why This Round Is Different From Every Other AI Round This Week
The week of September 21-25 2026 produced dozens of large AI funding rounds. Most of them were bets on AI applications — companies using AI to build products that serve end customers in specific verticals. Snorkel AI is a bet on AI infrastructure — the layer underneath applications, underneath models, underneath everything visible in the AI stack.
Infrastructure bets are structurally different from application bets. Applications compete on product quality, distribution and brand. Infrastructure competes on reliability, scale and switching costs. Once a frontier AI lab is using Snorkel’s data factory for its training runs, switching to a different supplier means rebuilding the data pipelines, re-establishing quality benchmarks and absorbing months of transition costs. That switching cost is a structural moat that application companies rarely achieve.
Snorkel’s 18x revenue growth is the commercial proof that frontier AI labs have decided it is the supplier they want. The $350 million round funds the capacity expansion required to serve the next wave of demand as model training cycles accelerate and the number of frontier labs globally continues to grow. Annualized revenue run rate $375 million — eighteenfold increase in 12 months. Builds training datasets, evaluation frameworks and RL environments for frontier AI labs, hyperscalers and US government. Shift from labelling automation to finished data products. data.title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Cybersecurity, AI And Health Take The Lead
data.ai_summary: Ten U.S. startups raised over $100 million each in a week, led by two $400 million cybersecurity rounds for Island and Cyera. Other deals included $350 million for Snorkel AI, $311 million for Enveda, and $250 million for Precision Neuroscience.
data.author: Joanna Glasner
data.full_text:

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.

This week delivered a bountiful supply of big startup funding rounds, led by two $400 million financings for cybersecurity unicorns Island and Cyera. Rounding out the week were large financings for startups across hot sectors, including foundational AI, drug discovery, neurotech, and even rainmaking.

1. Island, $400M, cybersecurity: Island, a developer of tools for secure enterprise digital operations, raised $400 million in Series F financing. Evolution Equity Partners led the round, which set a $6.4 billion valuation for the Dallas-based company, more than double its 2024 valuation.

2. Cyera, $400M, cybersecurity: Cyera, a provider of enterprise data security tools that govern both humans and AI agents, picked up $400 million in Series G extension funding led by Evolution Equity Partners and backed by Goldman Sachs Growth Equity. The round brings total funding for New York-based Cyera to $2.7 billion, per Crunchbase data.

3. Snorkel AI, $350M, foundational AI: San Francisco-based Snorkel AI, provider of tools for frontier labs and AI teams to develop specialized training data and environments, secured $350 million in Series E funding. Insight Partners and S32 led the round, valuing the 7-year-old company at $3.2 billion, and it now has more than $375 million in annual recurring revenue.

4. Enveda, $311M, biotech: Enveda, an AI-enabled drug discovery startup, closed on $311 million in Series E financing led by Catalio Capital Management and joined by a long list of new and existing investors. The round brings the Boulder, Colorado-based company’s total capital raised since inception to more than $845 million.

5. Precision Neuroscience, $250M, neurotech: New York-based Precision Neuroscience, a startup focused on brain-computer interface technology, secured $250 million in Series D funding with Pershing Square and the Ackman Oxman Institute as lead investors.

6. Hubble Network, $200M, wireless communications: Hubble Network, operator of a satellite network that extends connectivity to Bluetooth devices, pulled in $200 million in Series C funding. Smith Point Capital led the financing, which set a $1.6 billion valuation for the Seattle-based company.

7. Rightway, $155M, pharmacy benefits: New York-based Rightway, a provider of pharmacy benefits and care navigation services, raised $155 million in Series E funding led by Francisco Partners. The startup will use the financing in part to expand its AI capabilities.

8. (tied) Rainmaker, $100M, cloud seeding: El Segundo, California-based Rainmaker, a startup focused on atmospheric research and producing new freshwater through cloud seeding, picked up $100 million in Series B funding. The round includes investments from Noa, Upfront Ventures, DCVC, Lowercarbon Capital and Dream Ventures.

8. (tied) Numeral, $100M, tax compliance: San Francisco-based Numeral, an AI-powered sales tax compliance platform, closed on a $100 million Series C round led by Insight Partners.

8. (tied) Micro1, $100M, AI data: San Francisco-based Micro1, a provider of AI training data to major AI labs, has reportedly raised a fresh funding round of more than $100 million at a valuation of $4 billion, according to a Forbes article citing people familiar with the deal.

Methodology

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Sept. 19-25, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

data.title: Snorkel AI's $350M Funding Highlights Industry Shift Toward AI Data Solutions
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation in a Series E led by Insight Partners and S32. The company's annualized revenue run rate reached $375 million, an 18-fold increase, as it expands from data labeling to data-as-a-service.
data.author: Win Warfield
data.full_text: Snorkel AI has raised $350 million in new funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, a jump that reflects how quickly demand for high-quality AI training data has intensified across the industry, according to TechCrunch, and a company announcement from co-founder and CEO Alex Ratner. The Series E round was led by New York’s Insight Partners and S32, formerly known as Section 32, with backing from existing investors including Addition, Lightspeed, Greylock, GV and Wells Fargo. The new valuation is nearly triple the $1.3 billion mark Snorkel reached 17 months ago when it raised a $100 million Series D, underscoring how rapidly investor enthusiasm has shifted toward companies selling the infrastructure behind AI models. Founded from research at a Stanford AI lab, Snorkel launched commercially in 2019 after four years of development. What began as a niche tool for making data labeling more efficient has evolved into a larger bet that the most valuable layer in AI may not just be models, but the data pipelines that feed them. Besides Ratner, the other co-founders of Snorkel AI are Christopher Ré, Paroma Varma, Braden Hancock and Henry Ehrenberg. Ratner completed his Ph.D. at Stanford University and is also an affiliate assistant professor at the University of Washington. Snorkel originally built software to automate data labeling, but the company has since moved into a broader business it describes as data-as-a-service. Instead of selling only tools for humans to label examples, it now delivers finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments that are assembled through a mix of software, synthetic data generation and subject matter experts. That approach is designed to serve frontier labs, hyperscalers, enterprise customers, vertical AI companies and U.S. government agencies, Ratner said in the company’s announcement. The company said its annualized revenue run rate has reached $375 million, an 18-fold increase over the past year. That growth mirrors a wider boom in the market for AI data providers, as model developers seek more specialized, higher-quality training material to improve performance in increasingly competitive systems. Other startups in the space have also reported striking growth. Mercor said its gross annualized revenue has climbed to $2 billion, Handshake reached $1 billion earlier this year and TechCrunch reported that Micro1 had scaled to $500 million. Those figures, however, do not all mean the same thing. Several of these companies reportedly pay a large share of revenue to the experts doing the work, which means gross revenue can overstate the economic value retained by the business. Snorkel argues its model is different because the payments it makes to experts are reflected in cost of goods sold rather than in the headline annualized revenue figure. That distinction matters for investors comparing fast-growing AI data businesses, particularly as the market expands beyond simple labeling toward more complex products such as finished datasets and simulated environments. [Noah Wire Services helped in the writing of this article.]

画像に写っているものが猫か犬かを人手でラベル付けする。AI 学習データといえば長らくそうした単純作業を指していた。だが、業務を丸ごと任せるエージェント型の AI を鍛えようとすると、話が変わる。
保険の引受審査を任せるなら、申請書類を読み、社内規程に照らし、必要な追加情報を取りに行き、最後に判断根拠まで書かせる必要がある。どの手順が正しく、どこで間違えたのかを判定できる基準がなければ、そもそも訓練も評価もできない。
共同創業者兼 CEO の Alex Ratner 氏は、こうした専門家が設計するタスクや環境、採点基準を「Data 2.0」と呼び、人員を増やすだけでは解けない研究課題だと説明している。
Snorkel AI が提供するのは、その「作り方」ごと請け負うサービスだ。ツールを売って顧客に使ってもらうのではなく、専門家が関与してデータセット、ベンチマーク、評価、環境そのものを構築して納品する形態をとり、研究チームが定義した非独占のデータセットや環境を「Snorkel Data Series」として提供し、四半期ごとに更新すると案内している。
同社は、良いデータは集めるものではなく作るものだと表現する。具体的には、対象分野の専門家の知見に、タスク設計、プログラムによる自動チェック、校正された専門家レビュー、評価環境を組み合わせ、学習に使える測定可能なシグナルへと変換する。まずモデルがどこで失敗するかを評価し、その失敗に合わせてデータや環境を作り、また評価する。そうした反復を回す運用だと述べている。
分かりやすいのが「Enterprise environments」と呼ぶ製品群だ。企業の実際の業務フローを高い忠実度で再現した模擬環境の中で、AI エージェントに仕事をさせ、訓練と評価を行う。保険の引受審査を再現した環境では、一度目の試行で正解にたどり着けた割合（pass@1）が10.9%から42.0%へ改善したと同社は自社の計測結果として示している。

data.title: Snorkel AI triples valuation to $3.5 billion in $350M raise
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI closed $350 million in new funding, valuing the company at $3.5 billion. Annualized revenue run-rate now exceeds $350 million, up from about $20 million a year earlier. The company plans to use the capital for hiring, scaling enterprise and government work, and expanding into new verticals.
data.author: Camila Nogueira
data.full_text:
Share

CEO Alex Ratner said Snorkel AI has closed $350 million in new funding, putting the company's valuation at $3.5 billion as demand from frontier AI labs for increasingly complex training data and simulated environments accelerates. Insight Partners and S32 led the round, and existing backers Addition, Greylock and Wells Fargo also took part. Annualized revenue run-rate at the company now stands above $350 million, compared with roughly $20 million twelve months prior. That new figure is close to triple the $1.3 billion valuation Snorkel carried after its $100 million Series D round in May 2025, a raise that also debuted Snorkel Evaluate alongside an expert data-as-a-service product. Growth remains the priority for now, though Snorkel anticipates turning profitable this year. Plans for the new capital include hiring additional researchers and engineers, scaling up enterprise and government work, and building third-party AI evaluation services, plus expansion into fresh verticals and data categories. The company traces back to 2019, when a group of researchers exited Stanford's AI lab to start it. Snorkel initially sold software for labeling and managing training data before moving toward direct delivery of finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, a data-as-a-service line it opened in September 2025. Tens of thousands of specialists across disciplines such as coding, law and medicine make up Snorkel's network, and the company charges for the finished data products this group produces instead of billing hours worked. Ratner said the approach means contributors get paid more generously while margins stay protected. Coding data currently outpaces other categories in demand at the company. Snorkel refers to its offering as an "agentic data development platform," combining human specialists with thousands of purpose-built AI models and agents to construct and verify data quality. Specialists handle the design work, setting scenarios, tasks and grading rubrics, and automated systems take on most of the intensive review labor. Frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, enterprises and the U.S. federal government are among Snorkel's customers, the company said. On the balance between human and automated work, Ratner said human involvement isn't disappearing anytime soon, noting that all the data labs draw real value from will still carry some human input for the foreseeable future, even as the volume of that data increasingly depends on synthetic and automated methods to keep pace with rising complexity. S32 partner Andy Harrison, who co-led the funding round, summed up the shift: "Data is becoming more rare, more specialized, more difficult to find." This funding lands within a wave of investment that followed Meta's $14.3 billion acquisition of a 49 percent stake in Scale AI in June 2025. Competitors Surge AI and Mercor have likewise seen strong investor demand, backed by their own revenue growth.

data.title: Snorkel AI Raises $350 Million At $3.5 Billion Valuation To Expand Agentic Data Factory

data.author: Amit Chowdhry
data.full_text:
Snorkel AI, a San Francisco-based company developing advanced data infrastructure for artificial intelligence, has raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation in a financing round co-led by Insight Partners and S32. Existing investor Addition also participated significantly. The funding will support the expansion of Snorkel’s agentic data factory, which supplies the specialized datasets, environments, and evaluation frameworks used to train and assess increasingly sophisticated AI systems.

New investors in the round include March Capital, Blumberg Capital, Allegis Capital, Frontline, Standard, and Third Point Ventures.

Existing investors Greylock, Lightspeed, GV, Factory, Prosperity7, Walden Catalyst, and Wells Fargo also participated.

Snorkel plans to use the financing to increase its capacity to serve leading AI laboratories and enterprises while extending its research and technology into additional industries, AI modalities, and applications.

Founded in 2019 out of the Stanford AI Lab, Snorkel develops tools and services for building the specialized data required to improve advanced AI systems.

The company is expanding beyond conventional data labeling, which typically involves assigning categories or other relatively simple annotations to existing information.

Its newer offerings focus on what Snorkel describes as Data 2.0, an approach designed for advanced and agentic AI models that must complete complex, multistep tasks.

These systems require sophisticated training and evaluation materials, including realistic task environments, expert-developed instructions, and detailed assessment criteria.

Creating such materials can take highly qualified specialists hours or days, particularly in industries where accurate outcomes depend on substantial professional knowledge.

Snorkel’s agentic data factory combines expert human involvement with proprietary technology to produce these research-grade datasets and evaluation environments at greater scale.

The company works with leading AI laboratories and enterprises on data used for frontier model training, evaluation, and performance measurement.

Its expert Data-as-a-Service offering, launched in September 2025, addresses the growing demand for specialized data development among organizations building advanced AI systems.

Snorkel intends to expand this business into additional high-value sectors, including healthcare, law, and software engineering.

These industries require AI systems to perform complex tasks involving specialized knowledge, detailed reasoning, and accurate responses to information that may evolve throughout a workflow.

The new funding will also support development of Snorkel’s core research capabilities and enable the company to expand into additional types of data and model architectures.

Snorkel’s founding team has made extensive contributions to data-centric artificial intelligence. According to the company, its research includes more than 250 peer-reviewed papers with over 25,000 citations.

The company plans to continue supporting open research through initiatives such as its Open Benchmarks Grants program, which encourages the development of publicly available AI evaluation resources.

The financing provides additional resources as Snorkel expands its role in the development of training and evaluation infrastructure for frontier and enterprise AI.

KEY QUOTES:

“The teams pushing the frontier want a research data partner who pioneers the science of data development. That’s what Snorkel was built to be: the frontier lab for agentic data, combining human excellence with over a decade of research and technology.”

Alex Ratner, Co-Founder and CEO of Snorkel AI

“Snorkel’s research-grade approach to AI data, environments, and measurement is becoming an increasingly important ingredient in building capable and reliable AI systems – and their demonstrated growth at scale reflects that. We’re excited to back Alex and the team as they continue to bring their frontier AI data factory capabilities to longer-running, complex work in high value industries like healthcare, law, and software engineering.”

Lonne Jaffe, Managing Director at Insight Partners

“Snorkel’s expert-agentic environments create a unique flywheel between human expertise and AI, delivering data at the speed and quality that enables a new era of efficiency and accuracy for model development. Working with Snorkel ensures the highest frontier model success rate and creates a true partnership between model developer and data provider.”

Andy Harrison, CEO and General Partner of S32

Snorkel AI Raises $350 Million To Build Data Factory for Frontier AI Labs

By Ekemini 23 September 2026

Key Takeaways Snorkel AI secures $350M in a round co-led by Insight Partners and S32.

The startup leverages decade-long Stanford research to deliver programmatically constructed datasets for enterprise deployment.

The investment targets scaling agentic data factories for training complex frontier artificial intelligence systems.

AI models study data. Lots and lots of data. It was easier to train AI in the old days, but now, AI has progressed. More than labeling photos, you can now use AI to do virtually everything. So, it makes sense to create better and harder training models for today’s AI models. Snorkel AI raises $350 million to do this. This is what most people now call Data 2.0. Snorkel Raises $350M for The Data 2.0 Shift Snorkel AI announced it raised $350 million. The round was co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with a lot of help from existing investor Addition. New investors like March Capital, Blumberg Capital, Allegis Capital, Frontline, Standard, and Third Point Ventures also jumped in. Old investors like Greylock, Lightspeed, GV, Factory, Prosperity7, Walden Catalyst, and Wells Fargo joined too. With this new round, the company’s value stands at $3.5 billion. One year ago, its value stood at $1.3 billion after a successful raise of $100 million. Snorkel says its yearly revenue run rate has now crossed $350 million, all thanks to the launch of Expert Data-as-a-Service in September 2025. More Updates: Spott Raises $21M To Build AI Operating System for Recruiters How Does Snorkel AI Work? Imagine you want to turn an AI into a really good lawyer. You need two things. One, real lawyers who know how to create hard legal cases and write the correct answers and grading rules. Two, you need a way to check all that work fast and at scale. Snorkel built what they call an agentic data factory. It pairs tens of thousands of human experts with thousands of specialized AI agents. The human experts design the hard scenarios, the tasks, and the rubrics, meaning how to grade if the AI did it right. Then their own AI does the boring quality check work to make sure everything is perfect. So humans bring the brains, AI brings the speed. And the best part for the experts is how they get paid. Most old labeling companies pay people by the hour. Snorkel says they do not sell human labor; they sell the final data product. That lets them pay the experts way better while still keeping good profit for themselves. CEO Alex Ratner said the teams building the most advanced AI right now do not want just a vendor who gives them cheap labels. They want a research partner who actually understands the science of how to make good data. And that is what Snorkel wants to be, the frontier lab for data. This research has been on for over ten years, with hundreds of published papers already cited over 25,000 times. More Updates: HighLife Raises $90M For Europe Expansion and Study Who Are They Selling To? They’re selling to everyone who is serious about AI. Top AI labs, big cloud companies, new AI startups, big companies building their own AI, and even US government agencies. This is because everyone now has the same problem. Their models are getting so good that the simple data is no longer useful. They need harder and harder tests to keep improving. The $350 million will be used to expand its agentic data factory even more. More experts, more AI agents, and more complex environments where AI can practice. data.title: Snorkel AI Triples Valuation to $3.5B on Training Data Demand
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million in Series E funding on September 22, tripling its valuation to $3.5 billion. The data startup's annualized revenue run rate is $375 million, an eighteenfold increase over the past year. The company pivoted to data-as-a-service, combining synthetic data with expert contributions.
data.author: Abdul Wasay
data.full_text:
Snorkel AI raised $350 million in Series E funding on September 22. The data startup tripled its valuation to $3.5 billion in just seventeen months. This remarkable growth reflects an urgent crisis consuming the AI industry globally. Frontier models now hunger for training data faster than companies can provide it.

Insight Partners and S32 led the round alongside existing investors Addition, Lightspeed, Greylock, GV, and Wells Fargo. The seven-year-old startup originally provided software automating manual data labeling tasks. However, Snorkel shifted strategy last year toward data-as-a-service, delivering completed datasets directly. This pivot proved transformative for company growth and margins significantly.

The hybrid approach combines synthetic data generated by Snorkel’s models with subject matter expert contributions. This strategy differs fundamentally from pure human labor marketplaces operating today. Snorkel’s annualized revenue run rate now stands at $375 million. This represents an eighteenfold increase over the previous twelve months alone. Such explosive growth underscores how desperately AI labs need training data access.

Competing data companies are experiencing similar trajectories now. Mercor achieved $2 billion in gross annualized revenue. Handshake crossed the $1 billion milestone earlier this year. Micro1 scaled to $500 million gross run rate recently.

However, these figures merit careful interpretation because these companies pay 60-70% directly to domain specialists doing the work. Snorkel operates differently through its hybrid model structure. Its payments to human experts land in cost of goods sold rather than inflating headline revenue metrics.

CEO Alex Ratner co-founded Snorkel following four years researching at Stanford’s AI lab. The company launched commercially in 2019 with this academic foundation. Since then, Snorkel built deep relationships with major AI labs and corporations worldwide.

As frontier models scale toward trillion-parameter scales, training data demand grows exponentially. Snorkel positioned itself perfectly to capture this expanding opportunity through innovative data strategies.

data.title: Insight Partners, S32 back Snorkel AI at $3.5B valuation with $350M raise — TFN
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly triple its price 17 months ago. Its annualized revenue jumped from about $20 million to over $350 million in a year. The company expects to turn a profit this year.
data.author: Abhinaya Prabhu
data.full_text:
- Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly triple its price 17 months ago.
- Its annualised revenue jumped from roughly $20 million to more than $350 million in a year.
- The round underlines a broader shift: AI labs now pay for finished, expert-built data.
Snorkel AI just got a lot more expensive, and it’s not because it labels data faster than anyone else anymore. The company, which used to sell software for tagging training data, now builds and sells the finished datasets and simulated work environments that frontier labs train their models on.
That pivot has taken its annualised revenue from around $20 million a year ago to more than $350 million now, and investors have responded by tripling its valuation to $3.5 billion in a $350 million round.
Insight Partners and S32 co-led the raise, with existing backers Addition, Greylock, Wells Fargo, Lightspeed, GV and several others returning, alongside new investors including March Capital and Third Point Ventures. It brings Snorkel to nearly three times the $1.3 billion valuation it held after its $100 million round in May 2025.
From labelling software to a data factory
Snorkel was founded in 2019 by Alex Ratner, Chris Ré, Paroma Varma, Braden Hancock and Henry Ehrenberg, spinning out of Stanford’s AI Lab, where Ratner and Ré had built the original open-source Snorkel project. For years, the company sold tools that let enterprises label their own data.
Since launching a data-as-a-service business in September 2025, it has flipped that model: human specialists across coding, law and medicine now design tasks and grading rubrics, while a layer of AI models automates quality control, producing datasets and reinforcement-learning environments it sells directly to labs, hyperscalers, enterprises and the US federal government.
“Our strong view is that 100% of the data that labs will get value out of will have some human input in the foreseeable future. But 100% of that data will have to use synthetic and automated approaches to keep up with this complexity ,” said Ratner.
The data race is getting more competitive
Snorkel isn’t the only one cashing in on labs running out of usable internet text. Scale AI raised $1 billion at close to a $14 billion valuation before Meta later bought a 49% stake worth roughly $14.3 billion. Mercor went from a $30 million seed round to a $10 billion valuation on a similar bet, and has since been in talks to double that again. Surge AI, meanwhile, was reportedly weighing a first-ever outside raise at north of $25 billion.
Snorkel’s pitch against that crowd is that it designs the tasks and grades the output, which is a harder thing to compete away on price.
Snorkel says the capital will fund more researchers and engineers, expand its enterprise and government business, support third-party model evaluations, and push into new industries and data formats. It expects to turn a profit this year.
“Data is becoming more rare, more specialized, more difficult to find. If you want to train the most frontier, complex and capable models, now you need superior data,” said Andy Harrison, partner at S32 who co-led the funding.
If the last 18 months were about labs discovering they’d run out of internet to scrape, the next stretch is about who gets paid to manufacture what’s missing. Snorkel just put $3.5 billion that it can be the one doing the manufacturing — the harder question is whether that job stays defensible once every well-funded rival is building the same expert-plus-AI pitch.

data.author: Maria Deutscher
data.full_text:
Training data provider Snorkel AI raises $350M at $3.5B valuation
Snorkel AI Inc., a provider of artificial intelligence training data, today disclosed that it has raised $350 million in funding.
Insight and S32 led the Series E deal. They were joined by more than a half-dozen other backers including Alphabet Inc.’s GV startup fund.
Snorkel AI was founded in 2019 by researchers from the Stanford AI Lab. Its first product was Snorkel Flow, a software platform that reduced the amount of work involved in supervised learning projects. Supervised learning is an AI development method that trains neural networks using labeled datasets. Such files comprise prompts and correct, human-generated answers to those prompts.
Creating labeled datasets is a highly time-consuming process. Snorkel Flow automated the process using statistical methods developed by the company’s founders at Stanford. According to Snorkel AI, those methods addressed the accuracy issues that made earlier automation approaches ineffective.
Last year, the company changed its business model. It pivoted from selling software that helps developers create training data to providing ready-to-use training datasets. Additionally, Snorkel AI expanded its focus beyond supervised learning to a second, more complex AI training approach known as reinforcement learning.
Whereas supervised learning uses datasets that contain prompts and correct answers to those prompts, reinforcement learning datasets contain unanswered questions. The AI model being trained must figure how to answer them without any human assistance. Once it produces a response, human reviewers or an automated system verify its accuracy. They then provide the AI with feedback that helps improve its reasoning.
Snorkel AI relies on tens of thousands of human experts to generate reinforcement learning training tasks. The company also provides customers with other technical assets that are needed for AI training runs.
When an AI model completes a reinforcement learning task, human reviewers check its work based on predefined evaluation criteria. Those criteria can span several pages. In the case of a programming task, for example, the evaluation guidance must cover all the cybersecurity and performance requirements that AI-generated code must meet.
Snorkel AI develops AI evaluation rubrics for customers. Furthermore, it improves those rubrics over time based on feedback from the human AI reviewers who use them. Some of that feedback is generated when two human reviewers give different scores to an AI prompt response. Such differences usually point to an inconsistency in the underlying evaluation criteria.
AI models are often trained in specialized virtual environments. A code generation model, for example, might require a simulated version of a developer workstation. Snorkel AI provides such as training sandboxes alongside its datasets and evaluation rubrics.
“Since launching our new data-as-a-service offering nearly a year ago, we’ve grown over 18 times, and this week crossed an annualized revenue run rate of $375 million,” co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Alex Ratner detailed in a blog post.
The company will reportedly use its newly raised funding to hire more engineers. Snorkel AI also plans to invest in AI safety initiatives and support the development of open-source model evaluation benchmarks.

Delighted to welcome Hesham Mahran, CEO and managing director of Orange Egypt, as a guest speaker at the 2026 EnterpriseAM Egypt Forum — the AI edition.

Appointed in August 2025, Mahran brings more than 27 years of experience across telecommunications, ICT, and digital transformation. As a long-standing Orange Egypt leader, he previously served as Chief Business Officer, driving the company’s expansion into cloud, cybersecurity, IoT, and enterprise connectivity. Under his leadership, Orange Egypt has become a key partner in Egypt’s digital transformation agenda, including “Ask Mariam,” Egypt’s first AI-powered airport assistant at Cairo International Airport. He has also been closely tied to national infrastructure projects and smart city development, including the New Administrative Capital Data Center.

Join us on 5 October in Cairo. Attendance is by invitation only, and we're close to full capacity.

Request your invitation here.

Better handled at home

The National Bank of Egypt (NBE) secured preliminary approval from the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) to acquire Banque Misr’s branches in the Emirates, the two state-owned lenders said in a joint statement (pdf). The banks called it a preliminary agreement to integrate their overseas banking presence into a single operation under UAE rules.

IN CONTEXT- Those are the same branches the US Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) proposed on 28 August to cut off from correspondent banking access to American institutions, though the decision is not yet finalized and a 30-day public comment window is still open. The US regulator alleges the branches moved some USD 1.8 bn between January 2024 and June 2026 for 103 companies it links to Iranian shadow-banking networks. The proposed measure targets only the UAE branches. Banque Misr’s Egypt business and other overseas operations are not affected, the Central Bank of Egypt said at the time. The CBUAE launched its own investigation of the branches, looking at the same period covered by the US allegations.

Why it matters: The statement makes no reference to the US measure, though the transfer looks like a way out of it. Moving the branches to NBE offers a regulatory route to dealing with the FinCEN proposal and is “possibly the only one available right now,” banking analyst Hany Abou El Fotouh tells EnterpriseAM. He says it’s hard to see the move happening without prior coordination between the two central banks. “Customer rights and obligations would move with the branches to NBE, leaving it responsible for compliance going forward,” he adds.

“A purely political solution” is how Motaz El Dreny, founding partner of Dreny & Co., describes the acquisition. Without it, Banque Misr would have exited the UAE entirely, leaving no Egyptian banking presence there. He says the acquisition was likely proposed by the UAE side itself and that NBE was chosen “because it is the only bank capable of the acquisition, based on the unity of ownership” — both are fully state-owned.

The US Federal Reserve was likely briefed on the solutions under consideration, El Dreny says, to “confirm whether this solution achieves its purpose, which is lifting the sanctions.” He stops short of declaring the sanctions will be dropped but says “logic and reason indicate this step would not have been taken unless it was among the proposed solutions that would effectively lead to lifting the sanctions.” The speed of the CBUAE’s preliminary approval signals the urgency of presenting this to the Fed for final clearance, he argues.

Whether the move makes sense for NBE is another question. The banks have put no price, timeline, or branch count on the transaction, and Abou El Fotouh says the regulatory costs of taking on an operation under scrutiny could outweigh the return. With both lenders wholly state-owned, he sees it as moving assets from one state pocket to another, with the earnings landing in the state budget either way.

More to go around

Misr Life Ins. could have 5 bn shares on its register by the time it floats, up from 500 mn today. Last Thursday, the company’s board approved a 10-for-1 split that cuts nominal value to EGP 1 from 10 while leaving issued capital untouched at EGP 5 bn, according to a bourse filing (pdf) dated 21 September. That puts issued capital at half the EGP 10 bn authorized ceiling set by Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) Resolution No. 363 in February. The board also authorized the chairman to issue the call for an extraordinary general assembly within a week of the disclosure hitting the EGX screen.

What this could mean: The disclosure does not mention retail or the stake on offer, but expanding the share count before pricing leaves room for a broader retail offering in a market where individual investors drive the bulk of daily turnover.

ICYMI- Misr Life Ins. has been temporarily listed on the EGX since March but is not yet trading. EFG Hermes was tapped in May to manage the sale of up to 20% of the company. A fair value study was due by end-September, with FRA sign-off the next step before the government sets the final stake and timetable.

ATMs, meet the tax man

The Finance Ministry settled with the Federation of Egyptian Banks how bank ATMs are treated under the property tax, ending years of disputes with several banks, a government official and a banking source at the federation tell EnterpriseAM. The Tax Authority found banks were applying the Real Estate Tax Law inconsistently to their machines.

Bank premises were never the argument — they are taxable. The dispute was over the ATMs, and whether machines scattered across the country count as fixed assets the bank owns. The agreement lands on treating an ATM as movable real estate property, making it taxable as such. The new instructions aim to prevent repeat disputes and eliminate tax rulings that could be vulnerable to regulatory challenge, the sources say.

Three cases now decide liability, under instructions EnterpriseAM has seen:

Machines inside bank buildings are exempt to avoid double taxation, since the building is already taxed;

are exempt to avoid double taxation, since the building is already taxed; Machines placed in a building or property for a fee are taxable whether or not tax is due on the property itself or its shopfronts;

are taxable whether or not tax is due on the property itself or its shopfronts; Standalone machines are taxed as independent assets.

The clock explains the timing: Banks have until 30 September to register and claim the tax discount under the facilitations package, which runs to a 10% deduction on non-residential property for filing on time. Law 3 of 2026, which amends the 2008 law, took effect on 3 April and also gave taxpayers six months to pay outstanding property tax and qualify for a waiver of late-payment charges, and allows settlement of disputes before appeal committees or the courts at any stage by paying 70% of the disputed amount. Tax owed on buildings the RTA never inventoried or recorded is wiped for every period before 3 April, provided the owner files within a year of that date.

What’s next: A large number of requests have gone in to push the registration deadline to the end of the year, the government source tells us. The same exercise is coming for telecom towers and oil fields — survey, register, update the data, and collect — with the same facilitations and a freeze on property tax disputes, our sources say. The ministry wants around EGP 18 bn in property tax this fiscal year, up from EGP 3.2 bn in FY 2025/26.

IN CONTEXT- The Finance Ministry has been on a property tax expansion drive all year, deploying field committees to inventory North Coast resorts. The ministry’s November 2025 inventory plan already flagged cell towers, electricity stations, and wastewater facilities for inclusion.

LNG to close out 2026

The Oil Ministry aims to secure roughly 35 LNG deliveries for 4Q 2026 via a flexible import plan, Al Borsa reports, citing unnamed sources. The import mechanism adjusts contracted volumes based on local output and demand to address sudden energy fluctuations. While the sources did not specify where the cargoes would come from, they said that Egypt has recently prioritized US gas imports to leverage flexible delivery schedules and favorable payment terms that ease foreign currency pressure.

A trend of great import: Plummeting domestic gas production — down roughly 37% from 2023 to 2026 — forced Egypt to rely on more expensive LNG imports, driving a 36% y-o-y import surge in 1Q 2026. Securing medium-term LNG supplies helps Egypt reduce reliance on the spot market amid instability from the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine.

WEATHER- It’s another kind of summer day in Cairo today, with a high of 32°C and a low of 23°C, according to our favorite weather app.

It’s the same temperature in Alexandria, with a high of 32°C and a low of 22°C.

The big story abroad

The UN General Assembly meeting in New York has unsurprisingly dominated headlines. A key development was a three-hour meeting between US officials and Iranian envoys, which US President Donald Trump characterized as productive. This was the first direct US-Iran meeting since June, reviving hopes of a diplomatic resolution, despite threats by Trump to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic.

AI war spawns modestly priced models: Leading AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI launched more affordable AI models yesterday, responding to rising pressure from budget-friendly, open-weight rivals. OpenAI introduced the GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna — models with a 50% API price cut compared to GPT-5.6 — while Anthropic launched Claude Opus 5.5, offering a more token-efficient model that costs roughly 40% less to run than Opus 5.

New startup lands in AI space: San Francisco-based data startup Snorkel AI has secured USD 350 mn in new funding at a USD 3.5 bn valuation, driven by surging demand from frontier AI labs for complex training data and simulation environments. Snorkel's new agentic data platform pairs human experts with thousands of AI agents to automate dataset creation and quality control for frontier labs.

data.title: The pivot behind Snorkel AI's $3.5 billion valuation
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly tripling its May 2025 valuation. Its annualized revenue run-rate crossed $350 million, up from about $20 million a year earlier, after pivoting to data-as-a-service. The company expects to reach profitability this year, but renewal risk remains.
data.author: Anders Mirofollow
data.full_text:
The headline number hides the one that matters. Snorkel AI, a Redwood City data startup spun out of the Stanford AI lab, raised $350 million in fresh funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly triple the $1.3 billion valuation investors set in May 2025. But the figure underneath is the striking one: its annualized revenue run-rate crossed $350 million this year, up from roughly $20 million a year earlier. A company does not grow like that by doing more of the same. It grew like that by changing what it sells.

For most of its life, Snorkel sold software861053--. Its programmatic labeling tools — which let a data team turn an expert's rules into training data instead of hand-annotating every example — built a respectable enterprise business and, in May 2025, a $100 million round led by Addition. Then, in September 2025, it added a "data-as-a-service" offering: finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, sold as products rather than as a tool to build them. That pivot is the entire story of the tripling. What changed is not just the growth rate but what the revenue line measures and who pays for it.

The new customers are the most concentrated, best-capitalized buyers in technology: frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, enterprises, and the U.S. federal government. Demand has centered on coding data, with law and medicine behind it. To produce it, Snorkel draws on a network of tens of thousands of specialists in those fields, working alongside a fleet of specialized AI agents.

Here is where a careful reader should slow down, because one accounting choice does real work. Snorkel does not charge customers for human labor. It sells the finished data, and payments to its experts sit in cost of goods sold — below the revenue line. Its $350 million run-rate is therefore a top-line figure: that largest cost is recorded as an expense below the revenue line, not subtracted from the headline number. Not every rival reports it that way: the pass-through competitors in this space hand 60% to 70% of their top-line income to outside specialists, so a same-sized gross number from one of them overstates how much value it keeps. This is part of why Snorkel expects to reach profitability this year even while growing this fast.

The catch is that it is still a services business, and a services business captures value only as long as the customer keeps buying. The cleanliness of the accounting does not tell you whether a frontier lab will renew at these prices a year from now — whether Snorkel's data measurably improves its models, or whether a customer worth tens of billions decides it would rather own the capability. That last risk is live. Meta's June 2025 purchase of a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.3 billion shows how high the data bottleneck has risen, and how willing the biggest AI spenders are to buy their way into it. The concentration that makes Snorkel's customers rich enough to pay also makes them powerful enough to internalize the work or fund a competitor.

Work through the arithmetic and the round looks ordinary for the category. A $3.5 billion valuation against a $350 million run-rate is roughly ten times revenue, unremarkable for a hypergrowth AI infrastructureAIIA-- name. The valuation tripled not because ten times became extraordinary but because the revenue in the denominator grew about seventeenfold in a year. An investor's honest question is not whether the multiple is rich. It is whether the revenue is real and repeatable. It is real in that customers pay for finished data. Its repeatability is unproved, because a year-old services run-rate sold to a handful of hyperconcentrated buyers has not yet been tested through a single renewal cycle.

The round is a signal about the AI stack even for investors who will never own a share of Snorkel. Value has been sliding from raw compute toward the data that decides how good a model actually is, and a company that spent years as a modest labeling tool just converted that position into more than $350 million of annualized revenue in a year. The bullish case is a flywheel — human expertise training specialized agents that make the next dataset cheaper and better, so each renewal gets harder to walk away from. The case that fails it is a services business whose revenue rests on a few laboratories that could, at sufficient scale, build the capability themselves. What separates the two is not the tripled valuation but the one thing nine months of new revenue cannot yet show: whether the customers come back.

data.title: Snorkel AI's $3.5 Billion Round Looked Like a Re-Rating — It Was Actually a Discount
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, co-led by Insight Partners and S32. The company's annualized revenue crossed $350 million, down from $20 million a year prior, making the round a discount on sales. It expects to reach profitability this year.
data.author: Julian Cruzfollow
data.full_text:
After the close on Monday, private AI data company Snorkel AI said it had raised $350 million in fresh funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, in a round co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with existing investors Addition, Greylock and Wells Fargo participating.

On its face that reads like a startup in escape velocity — nearly three times the $1.3 billion Snorkel fetched in its May 2025 round. But the more revealing math sits underneath, because on a sales basis the company actually got cheaper.

Here is the ledger. Annualized revenue has crossed $350 million, up from approximately $20 million a year prior. Divide today's $3.5 billion valuation by that roughly $350 million run-rate and you get about 10 times sales. Run the same divide on the May 2025 round — $1.3 billion on roughly $20 million of revenue — and you're at about 65 times. In absolute dollars the company nearly tripled in value; on revenue it de-rated by a factor of more than six. That is not the shape of a bubble round. It's the shape of a company that grew into its number.

The reason the number moved so fast is that the business itself changed. Snorkel was founded in 2019 by Stanford AI lab researchers and built its name on software861053-- — Snorkel Flow, a programmatic data-labeling platform. For years that software model produced only modest revenue. Then, in September 2025, the company launched a data-as-a-service business: instead of selling tools, it began selling finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, and it sells the resulting data products rather than charging for human labor.

The pivot was a genuine break, not a cosmetic one. Right around that same launch, Snorkel cut 31 of about 240 employees — roughly 13% of the workforce — with software engineers hit hardest, as the company said it was deprioritizing legacy areas. You don't lay off your software engineers the month after launching the product you were built around unless the old model wasn't scaling. The layoff and the launch describe the same event from two directions.

All of which points at the question that matters for anyone sizing the AI data theme: is this data-as-a-service a product, or a services business in disguise? The bull case is that it leans toward product. Snorkel combines teams of human experts in coding, law and medicine with specialized AI models and agents for quality control, then sells the finished data; it does not bill for headcount. Cost it favorably and that could carry software-like margins, and Reuters reports the company expects to reach profitability this year.

The bear case is that any business built around expert humans carries heavier costs than a pure software license, and the public AI complex makes that tension visible. PalantirPLTR--, the closest big public AI software name, trades at roughly 72 times trailing sales with a gross margin near 85%, as of Monday's close. Against that, Snorkel at about 10 times forward run-rate looks cheap — but Palantir sells software and Snorkel sells data with a human-expert layer inside it. A discount to 72 times sales doesn't automatically mean fair value if the cost structure never reaches software margins. The whole gap between Snorkel's single-digit multiple and Palantir's 70-plus is a wager on how productized, and how margin-rich, "expert data" can actually get.

For an ordinary retail reader, the honest caveat is that you cannot buy Snorkel — it is privately held, and none of this re-rating is capturable in a brokerage account. What the round is, then, is a live data point on the AI supply chain: the market increasingly treats high-quality training and evaluation data as the binding constraint on frontier models, and it is willing to pay for the companies that produce it. The public way to express that bet runs through the AI software names, which already carry far richer multiples — so a private raise at about 10 times run-rate either validates the theme or is a reminder of how extended the public AI complex has become. It can be both.

When I rank the live issues here, valuation is not the one that worries me. At roughly 10 times a growing, near-breakeven run-rate, the price looks defensible even if the dollar figure in the headline is big. The larger question is the durability and the margins of the data-as-a-service model, which is barely a year old and, by the company's own accounting, only just approaching profitability. I'd take the round as real evidence that the AI data layer is a competitive bottleneck worth watching, but I'd want to see proof that a human-expert data business can hold software-like margins across a few more quarters of scale before giving it the benefit of the doubt. Profitability is expected this year, not yet delivered.

A company that priced itself at $1.3 billion a year ago just raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation in a round led by InsightNSIT-- and S32, roughly tripling the $1.3 billion valuation it set in May 2025. Read like every other frothy AI headline, this looks like a data-labeling startup re-rating on narrative momentum. The math underneath says otherwise: Snorkel AI grew its revenue base faster than it grew its valuation, so the tripling actually made each dollar of its sales cheaper to own. At the May 2025 round, Snorkel carried a $1.3 billion valuation on about $20 million in revenue — a 65x multiple on a company that sold software861053--. Twelve months later, annualized revenue has crossed $350 million, up from roughly $20 million a year earlier, a step the company describes as growth of more than 18x. Try the division yourself: take the new $3.5 billion valuation and divide by roughly $350 million of revenue, and the multiple lands near 10x. The price tag tripled while the multiple fell by more than 80 percent, because revenue compounded far faster than the number on the term sheet changed. What produced that step-change is a change in what the company sells. Instead of licensing data-labeling software, Snorkel now supplies the finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments that frontier models are actually trained on, a data-as-a-service offering launched in September 2025. The structure matters to returns: it sells data products rather than billing for human hours, so it can pay specialists well while machines handle the repetitive quality-control work. That a service launched less than a year ago now anchors a $350 million-plus annualized run rate is usage and real capital, not attention. The read-through for a retail investor needs one explicit warning: this is not a stock you can buy. The $3.5 billion figure is a private, negotiated price set by professional investors, not a public-market quote. What the round does hand an outsider is a map of where institutional money believes the AI bottleneck has moved — from compute toward the specialized data that trains, evaluates, and keeps models aligned. It is the difference between selling a labeling tool once and supplying the scarce data itself on a recurring basis, which is why funds pay a venture multiple for the second. Two limits should temper how far that logic carries. Every number above is company-reported from a private firm with no audited public disclosure, so a retail investor cannot verify the run rate. And the customer base is concentrated among frontier labs, hyperscalers, and the federal government, which makes a lab deciding to build data work in-house the single largest threat to the model. The company says it expects to reach profitability within the current year — that is the condition worth watching. If the run rate keeps compounding at these margins, a roughly 10x multiple has organic support; if growth decelerates sharply or a major customer pulls the work inside, there is no public bid standing by to catch the price. The honest judgment to take from the round is that the tripling is real, because it is carried by a revenue jump of roughly 17x rather than by a higher multiple. The open question is not whether Snorkel deserves more per dollar of sales than it did a year ago — it clearly does — but whether the data-as-a-service compound can keep clearing past $350 million and, eventually, at what price a public market chooses to value it. data.title: Venture Capital & Startup Funding Roundup, September 22, 2026: General Catalyst, Goldman Sachs, Greylock, M13, Y Combinator & More
data.ai_summary: Ten venture rounds totaling about $1.379 billion were announced on September 22, 2026, with Cyera, Snorkel AI, and Heidi Health leading. The headline capital includes $240 million non-dilutive financing from Heidi, leaving roughly $1.139 billion in equity. Investors are concentrating capital on companies controlling strategic bottlenecks in AI infrastructure.
data.author: Nickie Louise
data.full_text:
0 Shares

Venture capital today is clustering around a surprisingly consistent idea: the next layer of AI value is shifting away from the model itself and toward the systems that make AI usable, governable, trustworthy, and economically productive. Cybersecurity company Cyera pulled in another $400 million. Snorkel AI raised $350 million to supply increasingly specialized training data and reinforcement-learning environments. Heidi Health paired a $100 million equity round with a $240 million non-dilutive facility as clinical AI moves from transcription into healthcare workflows. That pattern continues further down the funding stack. Go.AI is putting private AI infrastructure inside regulated institutions. Firecrawl is building the data-access layer agents need to interact with the web. Baselayer is attacking financial fraud. Sela is applying voice agents specifically to mortgage sales, while Teal Health and Ramona Optics show that investors are still willing to finance differentiated healthcare and life-science infrastructure outside the generative-AI rush. Axios’ deal reporting captures the unusually dense cluster of enterprise AI, security, fintech and healthcare rounds announced Tuesday. Across the ten rounds selected below, the headline capital committed totals about $1.379 billion. That figure needs one qualification: $240 million of Heidi’s package is non-dilutive financing rather than equity, leaving roughly $1.139 billion of equity or equity-like venture/growth funding in the selected set. The three largest transactions, Cyera, Snorkel AI, and Heidi, account for about 79% of headline capital, or roughly three-quarters of the equity component. That concentration is the day’s clearest market signal: investors are writing very large checks where companies can demonstrate strategic control points, customer adoption or both. The Macro Environment: Capital Is Paying for Control, Not Just Intelligence The backdrop is not one of cheap money. The Federal Reserve raised its target range by 25 basis points on September 16 to 3.75%–4.00%, meaning venture investors are still competing against a meaningful cost of capital. That makes today’s nine-figure private rounds more revealing than they would be in a zero-rate environment: investors are reserving large checks for businesses they believe can either dominate a category or become infrastructure other businesses cannot easily remove. Cyera is a good example of the first category. Goldman Sachs is putting $400 million into a company already valued at more than $12 billion, shortly after Cyera completed its $1 billion acquisition of non-human-identity specialist Oasis Security. The investment is less about financing basic product development than giving Cyera enough balance-sheet latitude to broaden its platform, pursue federal and overseas customers, make acquisitions, and choose its own timing for a future public offering. The Wall Street Journal reports that Cyera has raised $1.94 billion since June 2025 alone and has now landed its first customer spending more than $10 million annually. Snorkel represents the second category: infrastructure underneath increasingly capable models. Its annualized revenue run-rate has risen from roughly $20 million a year ago to more than $350 million, according to Reuters, as frontier labs need harder training tasks, specialist-generated datasets and reinforcement-learning environments rather than commodity labeling. At a $3.5 billion valuation, the round prices Snorkel at roughly ten times its reported annualized revenue — a valuation that looks aggressive in ordinary software but much less unusual for a company growing at this speed and positioning itself directly in the frontier-model supply chain. We calculated that multiple from Reuters’ reported valuation and revenue figures. Private and public capital are also beginning to meet around AI infrastructure. On the same day these venture rounds surfaced, data-center infrastructure provider Accelevation set U.S. IPO terms at $20 to $24 per share, implying a market capitalization of around $4.9 billion at the midpoint. That does not mean the public market is broadly open to every venture-backed software company. It suggests something narrower: businesses connected to AI’s physical, security, and operational requirements have a more credible path toward institutional-scale financing than undifferentiated application companies. The implication for founders is important. Calling a product “AI-native” is not enough to command premium capital. Today’s stronger financings sit at specific bottlenecks: who can access sensitive data, where models run, how training data is generated, how clinical work is documented, how agents retrieve information, and how regulated transactions are verified. Investors appear increasingly willing to fund the companies that own those bottlenecks rather than another thin interface sitting on top of somebody else’s model. The Top Funding Rounds Cyera raises $400M to secure data and AI-agent access across the enterprise Cyera’s $400 million investment from Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives extends the company’s Series G and comes only months after a $600 million Series G valued the New York cybersecurity company at $12 billion. Cyera says the new investment will support its AI-security roadmap, federal-market expansion and continued growth across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific. The strategic premise has broadened substantially from classic data-security posture management. Enterprises deploying AI agents now have software identities that can call tools, query databases, and act on corporate information without constant human involvement. Cyera’s acquisition of Oasis Security brought non-human identity management into the same platform as data security, allowing the company to address both sides of the permission problem: where sensitive information sits and which human, machine or agent can reach it. That is also why Goldman entering at this stage is notable. This is late-stage capital going into a company that already has the scale to contemplate an IPO, not a speculative bet on whether a category will exist. The Wall Street Journal reports that Cyera’s newest financing gives it additional freedom to invest in products and M&A while delaying a listing if private capital remains attractive. For competing data-security and identity vendors, that creates a well-funded consolidator with both an acquisition currency and a $12 billion-plus valuation benchmark. Funding Details

Investors: Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives; existing Series G was led by Evolution Equity

The valuation is almost three times the $1.3 billion figure attached to Snorkel’s $100 million financing in May 2025. More striking is the operating trajectory: Reuters reports annualized revenue above $350 million, versus roughly $20 million a year earlier. The change is tied to a strategic pivot. Snorkel began as software for programmatic data labeling but has increasingly become a supplier of finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments. Its network includes specialists in coding, law and medicine, while AI systems automate portions of quality assurance and data production. CEO Alex Ratner argues that increasingly capable models require data that is harder to source and judge, creating demand for human expertise combined with automated production rather than conventional annotation labor. That places Snorkel in a market reshaped by Scale AI, Mercor, Surge AI and the frontier labs’ appetite for difficult training and evaluation data. Reuters notes that investor interest intensified after Meta’s 2025 purchase of a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.3 billion. Snorkel’s answer is to sell the data product rather than bill customers for hours of human work — potentially giving it better operating leverage if it can preserve quality as volumes rise. Blackbird led the equity financing, with Phoenix Court and, according to Axios, Point72 Private Investments and Headline participating; General Catalyst led the $240 million financing component. That moves the thesis beyond whether clinicians will use an ambient scribe: the harder question is whether one vendor can become part of the operating layer of large health systems. Valuation reporting differs slightly by outlet. The Times puts the latest valuation at about $900 million, while Australian coverage describes Heidi as reaching roughly the $1 billion or unicorn threshold. The discrepancy likely reflects rounding and reporting conventions, not two separate financings. The more important signal is the financing structure itself. Using $240 million of non-dilutive capital lets Heidi finance expansion without selling the same amount of ownership at today’s valuation — a playbook increasingly relevant to rapidly growing software companies with enough revenue visibility to support structured capital.
